headline: Warsh's non-answer in Bangkok cut Oct 28 hike odds to ≈15–17%, so the 10Y is holding near 5.07% after its best day since Aug 2025. The test now is whether regional banks, all beating on EPS, can keep the old-economy rotation going while AI credit stabilizes.
summary: Fed: Warsh told the IMF in Bangkok overnight that he won't pre-commit for any 2026 meeting. He praised 'synchronous' global tightening ('no free riders') and called AI's path 'very bumpy.' Hike odds for Oct 28 fell from ≈27–30% to ≈15–17% (FT/Bloomberg/CME), and Dec is still ≈90% priced. Goldman now expects an October pause and a December hike, and Citi also calls December. The blackout starts Saturday, so this is the last Fed word before the meeting.

Rates: the 2Y is 4.73%, the 10Y 5.07% and the 30Y 5.42% (CNBC, early), after Thursday's ≈9–13 bp bull rally on the 10Y from a 5.33% post-CPI high. Bunds are near 5-week lows at ≈3.40%, and the 10Y JGB is up 1.5 bp to 2.935% as risk-off eased in Asia. Import prices (7:30 CT, ≈+0.8–0.9% m/m) and industrial production (8:15 CT, +0.4%) are second-tier, but after a 6.3% y/y PPI a hot import print would hit the front end.

Banks: the Friday regionals beat on EPS. Citizens posted $1.41 vs $1.40 and raised its dividend 13%. Regions posted adjusted $0.73 vs ≈$0.66–0.67, with record capital-markets income and NCOs down to 0.29%. Truist posted adjusted $1.16 vs $1.12 but only $0.56 GAAP after a ≈$1.4B loss selling AFS securities to reinvest at higher yields, and it guided Q4 NII to $3.65–3.70B. M&T posted $5.04 with CET1 at 10.16% and 90-day-past-due loans up to $570M from $432M y/y.

Equities: ES is ≈+0.2%, Dow futures +145 pts and NQ ≈−0.2% (Invezz). That follows Thursday's Dow +1.08%, Russell +1.38% and Nasdaq flat. The rotation from AI megacaps into cyclicals and small caps is the trade into monthly opex. VIX is ≈16, but SKEW at 157 (Saxo) shows heavy demand for crash protection.

Commodities: spot gold is ≈$4,180 (+0.2%), on track for a ≈0.2–0.5% weekly dip, but the dollar's first weekly fall in five weeks (DXY ≈102.0) is a tailwind. Silver is ≈$57.9 (+0.8%), and LME copper is $14,462 (+0.8%) after a near two-week low. Brent is ≈$105.5 and WTI ≈$97.6, with WTI up ≈6% on the week as Hormuz flows run at 68% of normal (Kpler) and EIA showed an 8.6M bbl draw.

calendar.event: Truist, M&T, Regions, Citizens, Travelers Q3
calendar.why: All beat on EPS. Truist's ≈$1.4B AFS loss is the rate-sensitive story: it is selling low-coupon bonds to reinvest near 5%. Travelers posted core EPS of $9.18 and an 86.8% combined ratio.
This is the third hot-inflation risk of the week, after CPI and PPI. Oil above $100 runs straight through, and a beat would reprice Oct hike odds back up.
Goolsbee's overheating thesis is AI capex plus demand. Strong output would support the hawks.
Expiring hedges after a week of AI-credit stress can amplify or damp moves into the close. VIX options expire Oct 21.
Warsh's Bangkok remarks were the last word. From here, Fed-dated OIS and SOFR futures move on data alone.
This is the Chicago commercial-bank read. Look at deposit costs and loan growth with the 10Y above 5%. The call is Tue 10:00 CT.

calendar.event: 20Y bond reopening; CME Group, Northern Trust, Tesla Q3
calendar.why: The 20Y tail is the long-end demand test after the haven rally. CME should show record rates volume (Sep Treasury futures ADV 7.7M, OI 24M).
Markets have moved from >50% hike odds to pricing a pause. December is where the hike is priced.

rates.title: Warsh stays non-committal and October hike odds halve
rates.body: Speaking at the IMF in Bangkok, Warsh declined to say what he will do on Oct 28 or in December. He stressed price stability and welcomed coordinated global tightening. Oct hike odds fell to ≈15–17% from ≈27–30%. Goldman moved to an Oct pause and a Dec hike, and Citi joined the December camp.
rates.simple: The Fed chair had a chance to warn markets about a rate hike in two weeks and chose not to. Traders read his silence as a sign the Fed will probably wait until December. That calms short-term interest rates (what banks pay to borrow overnight), which feed into credit cards and business loans.

rates.title: 10Y holds near 5.07% after its biggest one-day drop since Aug 2025
rates.body: The 10Y is ≈5.07%, the 2Y 4.73% and the 30Y 5.42% in early trade, versus 5.33% intraday after Wednesday's CPI. Hot data (CPI 3.7% y/y, PPI 6.3% y/y) is up against a haven bid from the AI-credit scare. The 2s10s is ≈34 bp.
rates.simple: A Treasury yield is the interest the government pays to borrow. It fell this week because scared investors bought safe bonds, even though inflation data was bad. Those two forces now pull in opposite directions, so the next data surprise could move yields sharply either way.

rates.title: Global yields: Bunds near five-week lows, JGBs tick up
rates.body: The 10Y Bund is ≈3.40%, near its lowest in more than five weeks, and the 2Y Schatz is 3.059% after three straight daily falls. The 10Y JGB rose 1.5 bp to 2.935% (2.885% low) as Asian risk-off eased. The 10Y gilt is ≈5.36% (single source).
rates.simple: Government bond markets around the world move together. When fear about AI-linked debt spiked, investors bought German and Japanese bonds too. Japan's yields rising again today suggests some of that fear is fading.

derivatives.title: Front end reprices while long-dated vol barely moves
derivatives.body: On CPI day, one-day equity implied vol jumped by about a third while one-year vol barely moved. Oct hike pricing spiked above 50% intraday, then finished below 30%. The MOVE index fell 2% to 99.07 on Thursday as Treasuries rallied (Saxo).
derivatives.simple: Options prices show how much traders expect markets to swing. Traders paid up for protection against a big move on the day itself but didn't expect lasting turmoil. The MOVE index (a gauge of expected bond-market swings) dipped, so the bond market is calmer than the headlines suggest.

derivatives.title: SKEW at 157 into monthly opex
derivatives.body: SKEW hit 157.3, the highest in Saxo's series, while VIX sat at ≈16.9 Thursday and ≈16 this morning. Monthly options expire today, and VIX futures and options settle Oct 21. Front-month VIX futures were 17.68.
derivatives.simple: SKEW measures how much investors pay for insurance against a sudden crash, compared with ordinary swings. A record reading with a calm VIX means investors expect a quiet market on the surface but are quietly buying disaster protection, often around AI stocks.

derivatives.title: Hedgers position for a shallower hiking cycle; Dec ≈90% priced
derivatives.body: CME FedWatch has ≈89.5% for a December move. Newsquawk had ≈29 bp of Dec hikes priced earlier in the week, with EFFR at 3.88% and SOFR at 3.88–3.89%. Recent SOFR option flow has favored Mar-27 call spreads and Dec-26 put condors, which bet that hikes stop early.
derivatives.simple: SOFR futures are contracts that bet on where short-term rates will be. Traders are fairly sure of one more hike by December but are buying cheap bets that the Fed stops soon after. If the AI-debt scare spreads, those bets pay off.

metals.title: Gold eyes $4,200 as the dollar heads for its first weekly loss in five
metals.body: Spot gold is ≈$4,178–4,184 (+0.2%), still ≈0.2–0.5% lower on the week after the post-CPI low near $4,073. A weaker dollar (DXY ≈102.0, −0.5% Thu) and lower odds of an Oct hike are the support. The January record of ≈$5,589 is still ≈25% above.
metals.simple: Gold pays no interest, so it does better when rates are expected to stay lower and when the dollar weakens, since that makes gold cheaper for foreign buyers. Both happened after the Fed chair avoided signaling a hike.

metals.title: Silver rebounds but is still down ≈11% on the month
metals.body: Silver is ≈$57.9 (+0.8%) from $57.42 Thursday, after Wednesday's 6% plunge. Trading Economics shows it −11.4% over the past month. Platinum was ≈$1,610–1,617, having fallen ≈3.3% on Oct 14.
metals.simple: Silver swings harder than gold because it is both a precious metal and an industrial input for solar panels and electronics. Fears about slowing tech and factory demand hit it harder this month.

metals.title: LME copper bounces off a two-week low
metals.body: Three-month LME copper rose 0.8% to $14,462.50/t by 0959 GMT. Thursday's close was $14,309 (−0.88%), and the price is ≈$400 below September's record. SMM notes Chinese stocks are rebuilding and demand is soft at current prices, while Chile supply risk persists.
metals.simple: Copper goes into wiring, power grids and data centers, so its price is a read on global building and AI investment. China's buyers are pulling back at these high prices, but mine problems in Chile keep supply tight.

banking.title: Truist takes a ≈$1.4B securities loss to reset its balance sheet
banking.body: Adjusted EPS was $1.16 vs $1.12 consensus (+12% y/y), but GAAP EPS was $0.56 after selling AFS securities at a ≈$1.4B loss plus a $66M loss on the Regional Acceptance auto-loan sale. NII rose 1.1% q/q to $3.71B with a 3.00% NIM, and Q4 NII guidance is $3.65–3.70B. Shares edged lower on a revenue miss.
banking.simple: Banks bought lots of low-interest bonds when rates were near zero. Truist sold some at a loss now so it can buy new bonds paying about 5%. That costs it this quarter but raises future interest income, a common move when rates stay high.

banking.title: Regions beats on record capital-markets and treasury-management fees
banking.body: Adjusted EPS was $0.73 vs ≈$0.66–0.67 consensus (reported $0.71, $611M to common). NII rose 2% q/q to $1.30B with a 3.68% NIM. Capital-markets income rose 27% to a record, and NCOs fell to 0.29% from 0.42%.
banking.simple: Regions is a Southern commercial bank. It earned more by helping corporate clients raise money and manage cash, not just by lending. Fewer loans going bad means borrowers are holding up despite higher rates.

banking.title: Citizens earns $1.41 and raises its dividend 13%
banking.body: Net income was $636M (+29% y/y) and EPS $1.41 (+34% y/y) vs $1.40 consensus, with ROTCE at 15.1%. The Private Bank build-out added $0.16 to EPS.
banking.simple: Citizens is a Northeast bank that has been hiring teams to serve wealthy clients and their businesses. That bet now drives over a tenth of its profit, and the bigger dividend signals confidence.

banking.title: M&T: CRE-led loan growth, but late-stage delinquencies rise
banking.body: Net income was $775M, or $5.04/share, vs $5.32 in Q2. Average loans rose $2.6B, led by commercial real estate, and provisions rose to $135M. Accruing 90+ day past-due loans rose to $570M from $432M y/y. CET1 is 10.16%, and it bought back $323M of stock.
banking.simple: M&T lent more to commercial property owners, but more borrowers are three months behind on payments. That is an early warning sign worth tracking. Its capital cushion (CET1, the bank's core loss-absorbing equity) is still healthy enough to keep buying back shares.

banking.title: Schwab posts records, but the stock fell on guidance
banking.body: Thursday: adjusted EPS of $1.69 (+29%) vs $1.66 and revenue of $7.17B (+17%), just shy of $7.2B. NII rose 14% to ≈$3.5B, and core net new assets were a record $190.4B (+38%). Shares fell ≈4% pre-market Thursday as management guided toward the low end of full-year ranges.
banking.simple: Schwab earns much of its money on the gap between what it pays on customer cash and what it earns investing it. High rates help that, but investors wanted even more, so a strong quarter still disappointed.

cnbc.title: Warsh withholds a rate signal and praises global tightening
cnbc.body: Warsh gave no hint on Oct 28, said there are 'no free riders' in global tightening, and called AI's development path 'very bumpy.' Goldman now sees an October pause and a December hike.
cnbc.simple: The head of the Fed spoke at a global finance meeting and avoided saying whether rates will rise this month. Markets took that as a sign a hike is less likely soon, which eased borrowing-cost fears.

cnbc.title: Treasury yields inch lower as investors digest hot inflation
cnbc.body: The 10Y is 5.074%, the 30Y 5.422% and the 2Y 4.731% early Friday, after the week's CPI (3.7% y/y) and PPI (6.3% y/y) shocks.
cnbc.simple: Inflation came in hot this week, which normally pushes interest rates up. But investors fleeing risky tech stocks bought government bonds, which pushed rates down. Today they are drifting slightly lower.

cnbc.title: Gold gains on a softer dollar but heads for a weekly fall
cnbc.body: Spot gold is +0.2% at ≈$4,178 but down ≈0.5% on the week. The dollar is on course for its first weekly loss in five weeks.
cnbc.simple: A weaker dollar makes gold cheaper for buyers abroad, so the price ticked up. Gold is still slightly down for the week because of the hot inflation data earlier.

cnbc.title: Wholesale prices jump 6.3% annually, the biggest gain since 2022
cnbc.body: September PPI rose 1.3% m/m and 6.3% y/y, with core running hot. Thursday's market shrugged it off as the AI-credit scare dominated.
cnbc.simple: PPI tracks what businesses pay for goods and services before they reach consumers. A big jump usually shows up later in store prices, which is why the Fed watches it.

wsj.title: CoreWeave's slump spotlights the debt behind the AI boom
wsj.body: The WSJ's take on the AI-credit rout: CoreWeave's bonds yielded ≈15%, and CDS of ≈1,000 bp implies roughly a 60%+ five-year default probability before Thursday's partial rebound.
wsj.simple: CoreWeave rents out AI computing power and borrowed heavily to build data centers. When its bond prices crashed, it raised the question of whether the AI boom is being financed with too much debt.
wsj.source: WSJ via KELO (AP/WSJ syndication) and MarketScreener digest

wsj.title: Investors temper Anthropic IPO valuation expectations
wsj.body: The WSJ reports that investors are lowering valuation hopes for the planned listing as revenue growth slows. Estimates in other outlets range from ≈$1.5T to $2T+.
wsj.simple: Anthropic, an AI company, is expected to go public soon. Investors now think they may pay less per share than hoped, a sign the AI selloff is affecting even private companies.

wsj.title: WSJ odds: Oct hike ≈14% after Warsh
wsj.body: WSJ market-implied odds of an Oct 28 hike are ≈14%, close to CME's ≈15%, with the 10Y near 5.09%, well below this week's 5.3% peak.
wsj.simple: Traders' bets now say there is about a 1-in-7 chance the Fed raises rates this month. Earlier in the week those odds were above 50%.

tribune.title: Goolsbee: AI build-out may be overheating the economy
tribune.body: The Chicago Fed president called September CPI and PPI 'discouraging.' He said a 4% core inflation trend would be unacceptable and that inflation driven by AI capex or demand is more worrying than tariff or oil shocks, but he wants more data before backing hikes.
tribune.simple: Chicago's Fed president worries that spending on AI data centers is heating the economy and pushing prices up. If so, the Fed would need to raise rates further to cool it.

tribune.title: CME Group: record rates volume heading into Oct 21 earnings
tribune.body: September Treasury futures ADV was 7.7M, a September record, and Treasury futures OI hit 24M contracts. Q3 results come Oct 21, with consensus at $2.98 EPS and $1.71B revenue (MarketBeat).
tribune.simple: When interest rates are volatile, banks and funds trade more futures to hedge, and CME earns a fee on each contract. This year's rate swings have been very good for the Chicago exchange's business.

tribune.title: Diesel prices squeeze Chicago's economy
tribune.body: With Brent above $100 and Hormuz flows at ≈68% of normal, high diesel costs are hitting Chicago businesses well beyond farming and trucking.
tribune.simple: Diesel powers trucks, trains and machinery, so when it costs more, nearly everything that gets shipped costs more too. Chicago, as a freight hub, feels it quickly.

tribune.title: Wintrust and Northern Trust report next week
tribune.body: Wintrust reports Mon Oct 19 after the close (call Tue 10:00 CT). Northern Trust reports Wed Oct 21 pre-open, with consensus ≈$2.87 / $2.26B.
tribune.simple: These are Chicago's two biggest home-grown banks. One lends to local businesses, and the other manages money for wealthy clients and institutions. Their results show how high rates are affecting the local economy.

nyt.title: Bank of America fined $1B+ for lax oversight
nyt.body: The NYT's Oct 15 business front led with the penalty (≈$1.2B total, including a record OCC share of $750M). BAC fell ≈5% Wednesday.
nyt.simple: Regulators found Bank of America's internal controls too weak and fined it. The money matters less than the signal that supervisors are tightening up again.

nyt.title: China's exports surge toward a record trade surplus
nyt.body: The NYT reports that Chinese exports are surging, pushing the trade surplus toward a record.
nyt.simple: China is selling far more abroad than it buys. That keeps factories busy and supports demand for copper and other metals, but it also fuels trade friction with the US and Europe.

nyt.title: Social Security COLA set at 3.6% for 2027
nyt.body: Beneficiaries get a 3.6% raise next year, reflecting this year's re-acceleration in inflation (CPI 3.7% y/y in September).
nyt.simple: Social Security checks rise each year to keep up with prices. A bigger raise shows how much inflation has picked back up, and it also adds to federal spending and borrowing needs.

talking_points.topic: Why Truist sold bonds at a loss
talking_points.point: Truist booked a ≈$1.4B loss selling AFS securities to reinvest near 5%. Management says it adds ≈$40M to Q4 NII, a multi-year earn-back. With the 10Y around 5.07% after touching 5.33% this week, the timing of a repositioning trade is itself a rates call. Good question for a commercial-banking interviewer: how does the ALM team decide when the earn-back justifies the capital hit, and does a possible rally toward 4.75% change that math?

VIX is ≈16 while SKEW is at a record ≈157, and the MOVE index fell to ≈99 even as Oct hike odds swung from >50% to ≈15% in 48 hours. For an S&T conversation: hedgers are buying crash protection, not paying for broad vol. That fits a market whose risk is concentrated in AI credit (CoreWeave CDS ≈1,000–1,195 bp) rather than spread across the whole market.

Gold's ≈$110 round-trip this week (≈$4,073 post-CPI low, ≈$4,180 now) tracked the 10Y and the DXY almost tick for tick. That is a change from earlier in 2026, when central-bank buying made gold insensitive to rates. A metals-desk angle: with real yields high and Dec hikes priced, is the ≈25% gap to January's ≈$5,589 record a positioning flush or a regime change?

caveats: WSJ, NYT and the Chicago Tribune were not directly accessible, and page fetches failed this run, so every figure comes from search-result excerpts. WSJ items use MarketScreener digests and syndicated copies; NYT items come from the Oct 15 print-edition listing. The Chicago bucket uses Crain's, CME and StockTitan in place of the Tribune. Pre-market levels are approximate snapshots (≈5:30–6:20 AM CT). Oct hike odds differ by source (14–17%). The import-price consensus conflicts (+0.8% vs +0.9%). The gilt yield is single-source, and I didn't find a reliable KBW Bank Index reading.

updates.label: Close
updates.headline: The week ended on a tech-and-oil shock rather than a rates story. Brent hit $110 intraday and settled ≈$109.86 (+3.7%) as Iran stepped up Hormuz attacks, while the Nasdaq closed −2.1% and the Russell −1.7%, but the 10Y held ≈5.08%, about 15 bp lower on the week.
points: Equities close (TheStreet): S&P 500 7,659.44 (−1.09%), Nasdaq Comp 26,140.03 (−2.14%), Russell 2000 2,719.57 (−1.72%), Dow ≈−0.4/−0.5% (Yahoo). The S&P tech sector fell >3% and energy rose 2.5%. The S&P and Nasdaq posted weekly losses. Correction to the morning thesis: the cyclical rotation did not hold into opex, since only energy and the Dow's value names held up.

Oil reversed the midday dip and overturned the Midday tile (Brent ≈$105.3, down). CNBC has Brent touching $110, its first time there since May, and settling at $109.86 (+3.7%), with WTI at $101.41 (+3.5%). At least nine ships have been attacked near Hormuz since Sunday, and Kpler puts flows through the strait at 9.4 mb/d, ≈70% of the pre-war level. Ukraine's vow to hit Russian refineries added to it.

Rates: the long end barely moved despite oil. Investing.com's provisional 10Y close is ≈5.082% (day range 5.059–5.096%), and CNBC's last read had the 2Y at ≈4.73–4.76% and the 30Y at ≈5.42–5.44%. On the week the 10Y fell ≈15 bp from 5.24% on Oct 9, so haven demand and the fading odds of an October hike (≈16%, CME FedWatch) beat three hot inflation prints. One FXStreet-cited read put a December hike at ≈91%, which we have not verified. The risk is that $110 Brent feeds straight back into breakevens.

Metals: spot gold firmed late to ≈$4,198–4,200 (USAGold, Convex) from $4,165 at 9 AM ET, yet is still ≈−0.2% to −0.5% on the week (CNBC/Reuters). Silver ≈$58. The DXY is ≈101.5 (Investing.com, undated) and on track for its first weekly fall in five weeks. We found no afternoon copper print, so the ≈$6.56–6.60/lb tile is a morning read.

Banks: the Friday regionals all beat on EPS but missed on revenue. Truist made $1.42 adjusted vs $1.14 est. on $3.75B revenue, short on securities and loan-sale losses. Citizens made $1.41, two cents ahead, with revenue ≈$20M light. Share reads conflict (CFG anywhere from +1% to −5%). Next week: Fed blackout from Sat, Wintrust Mon PM, then the 20Y reopening plus CME Group and Northern Trust earnings on Wed Oct 21.
updates.simple: Oil jumped because Iran attacked more tankers near the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea lane that much of the world's oil passes through. Investors worry that fewer barrels will get out, and pricier oil means pricier gas and goods. Stocks, especially tech, fell, but bond yields (the interest the government pays to borrow) stayed put because investors still bought Treasuries as a safe place to park money. For banks and borrowers, that keeps loan rates high but not rising, while oil becomes the main inflation risk the Fed has to watch.

updates.label: Midday
updates.headline: The morning's rotation cracked by midday. The Dow gave back a ≈405-pt gain as a software selloff joined the chip rout, so the S&P is ≈−0.6% to −1.1% and the Nasdaq ≈−1.4% to −2%. Bonds stayed calm: the 10Y is near 5.07–5.10% and Oct 28 hike odds are ≈15–16%.
points: Equities: Yahoo Finance's 1:15 PM ET live post had the S&P ≈−0.6%, the Nasdaq 100 ≈−1.4% and the Dow ≈flat. Its quote panel was worse: S&P 7,657.75 (−1.11%), Dow 51,908.52 (−0.52%), Nasdaq Comp 26,182.78 (−1.98%), Russell 2000 2,730.43 (≈−1.3%). The S&P and Nasdaq are headed for weekly losses, while the Dow is still ≈+1% on the week.

What's driving it: software. Salesforce, ServiceNow and Atlassian are each down >3%, and 41 of the 45 names in Yahoo's software basket are falling, about $130B of market value gone. Chips are weak again too: Intel and AMD are ≈−3% and Nvidia is +0.4% at $218.10 (24/7 Wall St). Correction to the morning thesis: small caps are not carrying the cyclical rotation today, since the Russell has given back part of Thursday's +1.38%.

Rates: we found no clean midday Treasury print. CNBC's latest read has the 2Y at 4.731% (−1 bp), the 10Y at 5.074% (−1 bp) and the 30Y at 5.422% (≈flat), though its own data table shows a 10Y at 5.102% and a 30Y at 5.447%, so the long end may be drifting up. CME FedWatch has an Oct 28 hike at ≈16.1% (ActionForex), down from 27.7% Thursday, with a hold at ≈83.9%. That is unchanged since the Post-open update.

Commodities and FX: gold ≈$4,172–4,180 (Kitco early US trade, Mitrade), silver ≈$57.9, Brent ≈$105.3, WTI ≈$97.1, DXY ≈101.9 (Kitco), so the dollar is extending its first weekly fall in five weeks. The haven bid is going to bonds and gold, not the dollar.

Banks and deals: we found no new bank M&A today. The Friday regionals (TFC, RF, MTB, CFG) have no clean intraday reads in our searches. Watch whether the bank leg of the rotation survives the risk-off move into opex.
updates.simple: This morning investors were selling tech stocks and buying old-economy names like banks and industrials. By midday they were selling almost everything, led by software companies that sell products to businesses, so even the Dow's early gain disappeared. Bond yields (the interest rate the government pays to borrow) barely moved. That tells you the selling is about worries over AI-related spending and valuations, not about the Fed. Traders still expect the Fed to hold rates steady at its Oct 28 meeting.

sources.name: The Bold News / Kitco AM report

updates.label: Post-open
updates.headline: Both second-tier prints ran hot (import prices +1.1% vs +0.8%, IP +0.7% vs +0.4%), but the bond market shrugged: the 10Y briefly hit ≈5.12% then slipped back to ≈5.07%, and Oct 28 hold odds stayed ≈85%.
points: Import prices (Sep): +1.1% m/m vs ≈+0.8% consensus; Aug revised down to +0.5% (from +0.7%). The y/y rate is 8.1%, the steepest since Jul 2022, driven by fuel and the Middle East conflict (Reuters via syndication). That is the third hot inflation print this week after CPI and PPI (+1.3% m/m).

Industrial production (Sep): +0.7% vs +0.4%, the sixth straight gain. Utilities did most of it (+3.5%), manufacturing was in line at +0.3% and mining +0.2%. Capacity utilization hit 76.9% vs 76.5% expected (24/7 Wall St). That leans hawkish, but it is weather/utility-heavy rather than broad demand.

Rates: CNBC first showed the 10Y +3 bp at 5.119% with the 2Y at 4.749%. A later CNBC read had the 10Y −1 bp at 5.074% and the 2Y −1 bp at 4.731%. Haven demand on AI-credit worries is still outweighing the inflation data. CME FedWatch has an Oct 28 hold at ≈85.1%, essentially unchanged from the morning brief.

Equities at the open: Dow +0.4%, S&P +0.1%, Nasdaq −0.3% (Yahoo Finance live), so the cyclicals-over-tech rotation is continuing into opex. Truist traded ≈−0.9% to −2.5% pre-market on a revenue miss despite the EPS beat (Investing.com). We found no clean reads yet on RF, MTB or CFG.

Commodities: spot gold ≈$4,185 (+0.35%), silver ≈$57.9, COMEX copper ≈$6.56/lb, Brent ≈$105.7, WTI ≈$97.6, DXY ≈102.2. The morning thesis holds. Correction: the brief's 'hot import print would hit the front end' only showed up for a few minutes, as the 2Y gave it back within the hour.
updates.simple: Two government reports came in stronger than expected. One shows imported goods getting pricier (inflation), and the other shows factories and utilities producing more. Normally that pushes up bond yields (the interest rate the government pays to borrow), because it makes a Fed rate hike more likely. Today yields barely moved and then dipped. Investors are still buying Treasuries as a safe place to park money while they worry about AI-related debt, and traders still mostly expect the Fed to hold rates steady on Oct 28.
